e-470.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution with Inverse Sine
e-470.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\textrm{d}u = \arcsin(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of $u^2$ as the variable, we have $9x^2 = (3x)^2.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 3 \,\textrm d u=\textrm d x.
$$

We can now write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{9}{4\sqrt{1-9{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x)^{2}}}\,\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{1}{3}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{9}{12}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡3x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $25{x}^{2}=(5x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=5x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{\sqrt{1-25{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =5\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(5x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\text{d}u) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(5x)+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/9)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/9}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$  

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$

content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9\cdot (1-{x}^{2}/9)}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}/9}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

 

This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{3})}^{2}.$  

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{3}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x/3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot (3\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{x}{3})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for inverse sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(u)+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $9{x}^{2}=(3x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-9{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have $9{x}^{2}=(3x)^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=3x.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-9{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-(3x)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(3x)}{3}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
